entities.name: William IV, Lord of Egmont
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
William IV, Lord of Egmont (d. 1483), emerged as a pivotal figure in the Low Countries during the late 15th century, serving as Lord of Egmond, IJsselstein, Schoonderwoerd, and Haastrecht, and critically, as Stadtholder of Guelders. His career unfolded amidst the tumultuous expansion of the Burgundian State, a period marked by intense dynastic struggles and the consolidation of ducal power across the fragmented territories of the former Lotharingia. As a scion of one of Holland's most influential noble families, William IV's allegiances and military prowess were instrumental in extending Burgundian influence, particularly in the strategically vital Duchy of Guelders, a contested region on the eastern frontier of the Burgundian Netherlands.

His military and administrative career flourished under the patronage of Philip the Good and his formidable son, Charles the Bold. William IV distinguished himself in various campaigns, notably serving as an admiral during the Hook and Cod Wars, where his family traditionally sided with the Cod faction, representing the urban patriciate and nobility against the Hook faction's more populist leanings. In 1473, Charles the Bold appointed him Stadtholder of Guelders, a crucial role following the duchy's annexation by Burgundy. In this capacity, William IV was tasked with integrating the newly acquired territory into the Burgundian administrative structure, suppressing local resistance, and ensuring the duchy's loyalty to the ducal house, a mission he pursued with unwavering dedication until his death.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: William IV's loyal service as Stadtholder of Guelders played a crucial role in the Burgundian consolidation of the Low Countries, directly contributing to the administrative integration of a key duchy. His career strengthened one of the most powerful noble families in the region, whose influence persisted for centuries.
